title: The containment paradox: Why your ransomware playbook has the wrong people in charge
raw_text: I have sat in on a version of the same incident post-mortem in three sectors over the past two years. The script does not vary much. At 4:47 a.m. on a Saturday, an on-duty SOC analyst sees a ransomware payload spreading across three servers in the data center. The playbook says isolate. They hit the switch. Sixteen minutes later the CFO is on the phone: Those three servers were the production payment gateway. The malware would likely have reached a dozen more endpoints. The isolation took down revenue for fourteen hours. The Monday morning question from the board is not how the attacker got in. It is who, in the organization, was authorized to make a decision of this commercial magnitude at 4:47 in the morning. This is the question most incident response programs avoid putting in writing. The plan is documented. The SOC has it open on the second monitor. What is missing is the answer to a single question: Tho decides that a business-critical system goes offline and who carries the operational and financial consequences of that decision? In most playbooks I have reviewed, that authority is not assigned. It sits implicitly with whichever SOC analyst is on shift — typically someone who neither owns the affected business process nor can fully see the downstream consequences of the action they are about to take. This piece is about the gap between technical incident response and operational accountability. It introduces the containment paradox, the no-touch register as a governance instrument, a RACI structure for containment decisions and the answer to the most common objection — that a veto right will simply slow you down while attackers move. Why “isolate first” stopped being the safe default The classical incident response doctrine comes out of enterprise IT. It carries a reflex that used to be safely correct: When in doubt, isolate. A suspicious endpoint comes off the network. A compromised server is taken down. A flagged account is disabled. Fast action reduces dwell time, and reduced dwell time reduces damage. That logic is the spine of every SOAR default configuration and most IR runbooks. The doctrine breaks once isolation itself becomes the loss event. A disconnected workstation costs a knowledge worker a productive hour. A disconnected payment gateway, ERP backbone, identity provider, manufacturing line or trading platform costs revenue, contract penalties, regulatory exposure and trust — sometimes within minutes. The containment measure becomes the damage. It is no longer mitigation; it is escalation by another route. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report , drawing on more than 31,000 incidents across 145 countries, finds ransomware now present in 48 percent of all breaches — but also that 69 percent of victims chose not to pay and the median ransom dropped to $139,875. Read against incident-response practice, those numbers say two things: The trigger event is more common than ever, and the decisions that follow it carry more commercial weight than ever. Colonial Pipeline in May 2021 is the case study every CISO already knows but few have internalized correctly. The DarkSide ransomware was on the corporate billing system, not on the pipeline control network. Colonial shut down the pipeline anyway, because they could not guarantee the ransomware would stay on the IT side. The outage lasted six days, hit 17 states plus the District of Columbia and triggered the largest fuel supply crisis on the US East Coast in decades. The intrusion compromised a network. The response disabled a region. JBS followed the same pattern weeks later. A major US consumer goods manufacturer pursued a vendor lawsuit in 2023 arguing that the contractor had extended recovery time and was liable for the resulting downtime. Recovery duration is now an attributable damage figure in litigation. That shift was unthinkable a few years ago. The accountability and authority asymmetry In most enterprises, the executive responsible for the availability of a business service — the head of payments, the head of trading, the plant manager, the head of clinical systems — does not have the authority to prevent that service from being taken offline during an incident. The SOC has the authority. The business owner has the accountability. These are different people, often in different reporting lines, and the asymmetry only becomes visible when something is actually shut down. NIST’s SP 800-61 Revision 3 , finalized in April 2025 by Amy Nelson, Shanée Rekhi, Murugiah Souppaya and Karen Scarfone, restructures the entire incident response model around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 — moving the framing explicitly from “tactical execution” to “strategic alignment with broader risk management.” That shift is exactly the gap I am describing. The new doctrine treats incident response not as a SOC function but as an organizational risk-management activity in which the business owner is a named participant. This is not a problem that goes away with better SOC training. It is a governance problem. The asymmetry exists because the IR playbook was written by the security function, for the security function and never went through the legal and operational review that would have surfaced it. A SOC analyst at 4 a.m. on Saturday is not the right person to decide whether the company should lose fourteen hours of payments to prevent four hours of attacker dwell time. That decision belongs to a named operational owner — and if that owner cannot be reached in time, the playbook should specify a pre-agreed safe-state action, not let the analyst improvise. The no-touch register: A second reading of your crown jewels list Most security programs already maintain a crown jewels register — the inventory of systems whose loss would be existential. In its standard reading, the register drives investment, patch cadence, backup frequency and monitoring depth. That reading is right but incomplete. The same list has a second function that is at least as important: It is the inventory of systems your SOC must not touch without confirmation from a named business owner. I call this second function the no-touch register. It is not a separate database. It is the same crown jewels list with one additional column: For each asset, which containment actions are pre-authorized for the SOC to execute, and which actions require operational confirmation. The split looks something like this: Asset class SOC pre-authorized actions Veto-protected actions Payment gateway Detect, analyze, preserve evidence, monitor, restrict outbound traffic. Isolate from network, take service offline, force credential reset of operational accounts. Identity provider (IdP) Detect, enrich logs, alert on session anomalies, raise additional MFA. Disable federated trust, mass-revoke active sessions, force tenant-wide logout. Manufacturing control system Detect, passively monitor, escalate. Any action that could interrupt continuous process or trigger safety response. Clinical EHR backend Detect, restrict admin access, enhance logging. Take system offline, block clinician access, suspend data feeds to bedside devices. Standard endpoint (laptop, dev workstation) Full containment — isolate, image, re-provision. None. The point of the table is not the rows. It is the discipline of filling it out. In every engagement where I have run this exercise, the meeting itself produces the value: Business owners hear, often for the first time, that the IR playbook authorizes the SOC to take their service offline; the SOC hears, often for the first time, what the downstream cost of that action actually is. Most of the no-touch register is consensus once the conversation has happened. The artifact then makes that consensus enforceable. RACI for containment decisions Once a no-touch register exists, the RACI for veto-protected actions becomes straightforward. The model below aligns with the four-role logic that the Institute for Security and Technology’s Ransomware Task Force — a coalition of more than 60 organizations across government, industry and law enforcement — has repeatedly recommended in its progress reports: Containment authority belongs to the operational owner, not the security function alone. Role RACI Reason Business asset owner Accountable Holds both the availability mandate and the downstream commercial, safety or regulatory consequences of taking the service offline. Delegates operational confirmation to a named on-call lead but retains strategic responsibility. Security Operations Center Responsible Executes the containment measure once confirmation arrives or the defined escalation window elapses and the pre-agreed safe-state fallback applies. CISO / Head of Security Consulted Sets the methodological guardrails but is not the single-incident decision maker. Escalates to Accountable for enterprise-wide coordination on systemic incidents. Executive leadership / board Informed Receives a structured notification, not a real-time consultation. The Informed status is what makes post-incident reconstruction defensible in audit, regulatory review and litigation. In most enterprises this RACI line has never been filled in. The cost of that omission is invisible in normal operations and becomes existential during incident reconstruction — when an internal lessons-learned, a regulator, or a plaintiff asks who decided to take the system offline, on what basis and with what authority. The objection: Does this slow you down while attackers move? Every workshop on this topic produces the same pushback. If the SOC has to wait for a business owner’s confirmation, dwell time goes up, damage probability goes up and the veto right has effectively disarmed the response. Stated generally, this objection is correct. Stated about the no-touch register, it rests on three misunderstandings. The veto applies to a narrow asset class. The register covers the crown jewels — typically a small number per business unit, not the entire estate. Containing a compromised laptop is not veto-protected. Containing the identity provider that laptop authenticates against is. The veto-protected set is the intersection of assets whose loss is existential and actions that produce exactly that loss. The veto is time-bounded. A serviceable playbook defines the escalation chain with hard windows and a deliberate fallback action if the chain runs out. The structure looks like this: Step Escalation role Max wait Action if no response 1 On-call service owner (primary contact for the asset) 5 minutes Escalate to business asset owner. 2 Business asset owner 10 minutes Escalate to executive on call. 3 Executive on call (head of service line or COO delegate) 15 minutes Apply pre-agreed safe-state fallback — not unilateral isolation. The pre-agreed safe-state fallback is the design point most playbooks skip. It is not the original containment action executed unilaterally after the window closes. It is a separate, deliberately-designed action that brings the asset to a manageable state without forcing the SOC to improvise under pressure — degraded mode, read-only access, traffic restriction or whatever the business owner has pre-authorized in writing for exactly this case. The veto applies to actions, not detections. The SOC retains full authority to detect, enrich, preserve evidence, intensify monitoring and isolate every system not on the no-touch list. What is veto-protected is the small class of actions that would induce an unplanned outage of a continuous business service. Modern SOAR platforms handle this branching natively. CISA’s Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks, published under Executive Order 14028 and intended explicitly for private-sector adaptation, model exactly this kind of branched decision tree. The reason most enterprise implementations do not is not technical. The IR governance never asked them to. Three steps to implement, and one meeting that produces most of the value Implementing a no-touch register requires no new software, no additional headcount and no separate budget line. It requires four hours in a room with the right people and a willingness to write down decisions that were previously implicit. Build the register. Sit down with the business asset owners and identify the systems whose unplanned outage would be more damaging than the worst plausible cyber incident on those same systems. The list is shorter than most CISOs expect. The conversation is the actual outcome; the table is the artifact. Embed the security stop in the playbook that the SOC actually runs — not the playbook in the audit folder. Before any containment action against a register asset, insert a checkpoint: Confirmation by a named business role, defined escalation chain, defined maximum window, defined safe-state fallback if the window expires. Fill in the RACI. For containment of register assets: Business owner Accountable, SOC Responsible, CISO Consulted, executive leadership Informed. In most organizations this column has never been completed. Completing it is the precondition for being able to answer, after the incident, who decided what on which basis. The 4:47 a.m. test If I run only one diagnostic on a current IR program, this is the one. I ask: At 4:47 a.m. on a Saturday, with a credible ransomware payload spreading on three crown-jewel systems, is the SOC analyst authorized to take those systems offline on their own judgment? If yes, the governance has not yet caught up to the cost of that decision. If no, can the analyst reach a named accountable owner within a defined window, and is there a pre-agreed safe-state fallback if that window expires? If both answers are yes, the no-touch register exists in practice, even if it has not been named. If either answer is no, the gap is governance, not technology. The containment paradox is not solved by faster automation or by adding humans to the loop after the fact. It is solved by writing down, in advance and in plain language, who is authorized to take which business service offline — and what the response is when that person cannot be reached. The artifact is one page. The conversation that produces it is several hours. The cost of not having it is measured in the language of board reports, regulatory filings and discovery requests. title: How IT leaders can start the shift to quantum-safe security
raw_text:
For years, post-quantum cryptography was treated as a problem for a future leadership team. Important, yes, but still far enough away that many organisations could postpone the harder decisions for the next cycle.

That is changing rapidly. Over recent months, Google and Cloudflare have both set 2029 as a target for full post-quantum security across their infrastructure, driven by rapid advances in quantum research and a shrinking margin for delay. These are operational decisions made by companies that sit deep inside the global technology supply chain.

The same shift is now visible in national security. In her lecture at Bletchley Park, GCHQ director Anne Keast-Butler warned of a “narrowing window” for the UK and its allies to maintain their technological advantage as AI, cyber capabilities and quantum technologies advance at the same time.

From our work across standards bodies, regulated sectors and technology suppliers, the challenge now is coordination. Transition deadlines will only be met if semiconductor providers, OEMs, network security vendors and critical national infrastructure operators move in step.

That makes 2026 a critical year, when sector-specific Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) requirements need to become clear enough to shape procurement research and decisions and IT refresh cycles. Google’s 2029 commitment gives the market a real planning signal. As other hyperscalers follow, pressure will build quickly across the supply chain, especially for the vendors that the organisations that make up the Critical National Infrastructure (CNI) depends on most.

Supply chains will determine the pace of transition

Cloud and data centre hyperscalers and internet infrastructure providers sit at the centre of enormous digital ecosystems. When they accelerate post-quantum timelines, the effect moves through hardware manufacturers, software suppliers, managed service providers and eventually the organisations that depend on them.

This matters most in sectors with complex operational environments, including critical national infrastructure, financial services, energy and manufacturing. One unsupported system, one legacy platform or one unprepared supplier can slow progress across a much wider estate. For many organisations, success will depend on how well they coordinate across suppliers and how early they start turning broad policy goals into procurement requirements.

Progress starts inside existing change and budget cycles

One of the most common misconceptions about post-quantum migration is that nothing meaningful can happen until an organisation launches a dedicated transformation programme. In practice, that is rarely true.

Cloud migrations, infrastructure refreshes, application modernisation work and hardware replacement cycles are already under way across most enterprises. The organisations making progress are folding post-quantum readiness into these programmes as a resilience requirement, rather than setting it up as a separate initiative competing for attention and budget.

Replacing cryptography as part of a planned upgrade is cheaper and less disruptive than retrofitting it later under tighter deadlines. Every scheduled technology refresh is a chance to introduce quantum-safe capability, assess supplier roadmaps or retire systems that may become difficult to support later.

Prioritisation matters just as much. Organisations do not need to solve everything at once.They need to focus first on the systems that matter most, the dependencies that are hardest to replace and the points where delay would create the biggest operational and security risk.

Don’t let perfect be the enemy of good

A common reason organisations stall is the belief that they need a perfect answer before they can act.

A better starting point is to identify the suppliers and systems that matter most, and use that to set clear priorities. That can be done quickly through structured conversations across procurement, vendor risk and technical teams.

Once those priorities are in place, organisations can start measuring progress in ways that matter to the business. Vendor readiness, dependency concentration and coverage of critical services are more useful indicators than abstract discussion of algorithms. They show where resilience is improving, where gaps remain and where executive attention is still needed.

They also create momentum. When leaders can see real progress, they are far more likely to support the next phase of migration. Different suppliers will move at different speeds, but the broader transition will increasingly follow the path set by the largest providers and the sectors under the greatest regulatory pressure.

Post-quantum migration sits inside asset management, supplier governance and sound operational planning. The organisations that start early, set priorities clearly and coordinate across their supply chain will have more options, face less disruption and build greater confidence across the business.

Ben Packman is Chief Strategy Officer at PQShield

title: CW@60: The importance of a different path
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

My path was not the obvious route into fintech. I studied PPE at Oxford before joining Oliver Wyman as a strategy consultant. For five years I worked across Europe with organisations wrestling with digital transformation. Much of the work centred on familiar questions. How should established businesses respond to changing customer expectations? Which technologies mattered? What could be learnt from newer companies that seemed unburdened by legacy systems?

Increasingly, the answers pointed in one direction. The most interesting innovations were not emerging from incumbents but from technology companies that had reimagined old problems from first principles.

There were two reasons I found myself drawn towards the world of fintech. The first was observing the extraordinary pace of technological innovation in the US and becoming convinced that Europe would follow. The second was more personal. I found myself less interested in advising businesses about change, and more focused on understanding how products were actually built.

That curiosity was cemented in an unexpectedly ordinary moment.

My epiphany

In 2016, a friend showed me a new app called Revolut where you could hold multiple currencies within a single account and exchange them instantly. There was no dramatic product launch or keynote presentation. Yet I remember thinking not simply that the technology was impressive, but asking myself, why wasn't everyone doing this?

It was one of those moments that quietly rearranges your assumptions. Rather than imagining distant possibilities, I was looking at something that already existed and wondering why the rest of the industry still accepted so much unnecessary complexity.

A year later, I joined Revolut.

The transition could hardly have been greater. Consulting is designed around structure. There are established processes, extensive training and clearly defined ways of working. Revolut, at least when I joined nine years ago, was different. The company was small, fast-moving and often learning as it built. There was little time for elaborate onboarding because the work itself was moving too quickly.

I began in business development but gradually found myself gravitating towards product development. Building something from an idea, working alongside engineers, watching it evolve from concept to launch and then seeing customers use it fascinated me.

An innate interest

Looking back, I had been interested in the power of technology earlier in my life. At university, I considered journalism. What attracted me was not simply writing but understanding how something came into existence. How does a newspaper get published? Who decides what appears on the front page? How do hundreds of separate decisions become a finished product that lands on someone's doorstep each morning?

In technology, product development asks remarkably similar questions. How does software come into existence? How do individual decisions become a product that millions of people rely upon every day?

That curiosity feels even more relevant today.

Changing assumptions

For most of my life, the machinery of finance was invisible. Banking was something that happened behind counters, through forms, or after a spell of waiting. Businesses accepted these delays as part of commercial life. Opening an account took weeks. Expenses accumulated in envelopes. None of it seemed especially unusual because there was little against which to compare it.

That assumption has disappeared with remarkable speed.

Today, as head of Revolut Business, I can see that the biggest surprise has not been how much the company has changed, but how completely my own assumptions about business banking have been rewritten.

Technology has altered expectations in ways that are easy to overlook precisely because they have become ordinary. Today, someone can establish a business in less than a day, open an account without setting foot in a branch, reach customers around the world and manage finances from a phone while travelling between meetings.

Tasks that once demanded paperwork, patience and physical presence have become almost invisible. The best technology has a habit of doing that - it removes friction so completely that we forget it was ever there.

What’s next?

Artificial intelligence has dramatically lowered the barriers to creating software. Ten years ago, building a new product demanded specialist teams, substantial investment and considerable time. Today, an individual with an idea can move from concept to working prototype within days. The tools themselves are changing almost weekly.

This does not mean every idea will succeed, and actually probably means there will be more ideas that fail. Every significant technological shift brings its own questions and unintended consequences. But it does mean that far more people can participate in creating products than ever before. That feels like a profound change.

The same principle applies to business technology more broadly. Increasingly sophisticated tools are no longer reserved for the largest companies. Capabilities that once required sizeable budgets and dedicated departments are becoming accessible to businesses of every size. Whether through automation, integrated financial systems or intelligent software, technology is steadily removing work that adds little value and allowing people to spend more time on work that does.

That, ultimately, is what has kept me interested. Technology is not valuable because it is new. It is valuable because it changes what people are able to do.

When I first saw money move seamlessly between currencies in 2016, it felt like a glimpse into the future. Looking back, it was simply the beginning. The most significant advances quickly become part of everyday life, quietly changing expectations completely until we can scarcely remember how we worked without them.

James Gibson is head of Revolut Business.

title: Inside police plans to share intelligence and crime data across the UK
raw_text:
UK police are developing a national service for sharing local intelligence and police force data across the law enforcement and justice estate.

Announced by the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) earlier this year, the National Data Integration and Exploitation Service (NDIES) will allow local police forces to access and share data, including local force intelligence and digital forensics, from across the country.

Privacy campaigners have raised concerns that the project could facilitate artificial intelligence (AI)-powered analysis of bulk datasets of personal information which, when considered alongside facial recognition and other forms of real-time tracking, shows how “powerful” state surveillance apparatus is.

A “police data factory” within NDIES will incorporate data from over 50 law enforcement agencies, the Home Office, the Ministry of Justice, and “other” partners to provide them with access to a vast network of data for “analytical and reporting purposes”. These government departments will not be able to see operational data or intelligence itself, according to the NPCC.

Computer Weekly can also reveal exclusive details about key data exploitation systems used by several police forces expected to “plug into” NDIES datasets, including:

  • A planned national roll-out of software that will facilitate deep analysis of forensically extracted mobile phone data.
  • Internal Bedfordshire Police memos that admit there is a “medium risk” that a system provided by the US-based data analytics firm Palantir will potentially process personal data for purposes that are neither proportionate nor necessary.
  • Datasets feeding Bedfordshire Police’s Palantir system contain more than 1,000 records on people who haven’t been charged with crimes.

The National Data Integration and Exploitation Service

The National Data and Analytics Office (NDAO) within the NPCC is delivering the NDIES in collaboration with the Home Office. Kate Fisher-Stevens, director of the NDAO, has said the aim is “not to create a single national platform, collect more data or share it unnecessarily” but to “ensure data can be collated when necessary”.

“The creation of a centralised data infrastructure that supports cross-force, cross-system data sharing will be pivotal to that aim – creating a single version of the truth, with time, resource and subsequent cost significantly reduced,” she said.

In a pre-market engagement tender published last year, the capabilities for the NDIES were expected to cost between £75m and £250m over five years. Although no suppliers have been announced yet, documents obtained by Computer Weekly indicate that Palantir’s Foundry product is one of the preferred choices to meet these needs due to government and policing “interest”.

Design proposals for the delivery of police data integration and exploitation systems have also included plans to integrate criminal justice data with the Single Unique Identifiers being piloted by the Department for Education for child safeguarding.

Campaign groups have previously raised concerns with the Single Unique Identifiers as a child protection and crime reduction safeguarding initiative. The Traveller Movement, which advocates for Romany, Roma and Irish travellers, provided written evidence to Parliament warning that tracking children through these identifiers “could be perceived as an infringement on the privacy and autonomy of families who have historically faced marginalisation and excessive surveillance by public authorities”.

When asked if this has the potential to bring data on all school children into the hands of the police, the NPCC deferred the question to the Home Office, which in turn did not provide any answers.

The NDIES framework has been designed so that analytical tools can “plug into” national policing datasets to exploit the data. According to documents obtained by Computer Weekly under Freedom of Information laws, these tools appear to include an in-house system known as Prometheus and systems designed by Palantir and BAE Systems.

Exploitation of local policing intelligence and digital forensics, such as data extracted from mobile phones, will be central to the police’s plans, according to specifications seen by Computer Weekly.

A spokesperson and legal researcher from digital rights campaign group Privacy International said: “This is a step up in terms of how much data is being shared, and what forces across the board will be able to do with the data. It also opens up the possibility for using the data for predictive analytics.

“The amount of information that they can now collect and process, as they’re no longer having to dedicate human resources to this type of investigatory work, is alarming.”

Prometheus and Palantir Nectar: Data exploitation tools

Two key tools under development by the police are expected to play a key role in generating data and intelligence shared under the NDIES.

Computer Weekly has exclusive details about Prometheus, an “intelligence-only” system developed to aid analysis of digital devices seized from suspects.

Unlike tools such as Cellebrite, which decrypt and extract data from seized devices, Prometheus allows investigators to derive insights from the extracted data by cross-referencing it with other police systems. Personal data that police extract from mobile devices includes photos, text conversations and internet logs.

This allows investigators to build a picture of a case by identifying links and patterns between the data and existing police intelligence records. The outputs of intelligence-only systems are generally not admissible as evidence in court, however.

It is used primarily in child sexual abuse investigations so far, although there are plans to deploy it across a “far wider range” of offences.

Details of the system are considered so sensitive that the NPCC has not disclosed which five police forces are currently using it.

The NDAO’s Fisher-Stevens told Computer Weekly that a “number of forces have been involved in the development of Prometheus”, but she wouldn’t specify which, as this would “influence criminal tactics and significantly impact the interception of child sexual abuse”.

The NPCC refused to release details of the project’s collaborators, citing Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) exemptions that prevent the disclosure of information provided by or relating to the security bodies – for example, the National Crime Agency (NCA) or GCHQ.

The ultimate aim with Prometheus is national roll-out and availability to all police forces. It is currently live on the National Police Capability Environment, a web-based Microsoft Azure cloud platform.

Another tool currently being piloted by British police forces is Palantir Nectar. Bedfordshire Police contracted the US-based analytics firm Palantir Technologies to provide this service. It connects existing police data sources under a unified view, with underlying applications allowing investigators to exploit mobile phone data, profile individuals and process sensitive personal data with artificial intelligence.

It is built on the Palantir Foundry framework, the same system used in the NHS Federated Data Platform, which is an operating system that organises data and integrates it into specific analytics applications.

One application within Nectar called “Project Retrace” allows the police to map out locations an individual has visited based on troves of forensically extracted phone data, according to FOIA disclosures to Computer Weekly.

A Bedfordshire Police spokesperson refused to explain how this works. It’s unclear if the geolocation is based on cached data from apps that record your on-device location, by examining IP addresses that your phone has connected to, or through phone mast triangulation.

A spokesperson from digital rights group Privacy International said the police collect this data “through mobile phone extraction, cloud extraction, requesting information from mobile networks, and by purchasing data from data brokers”.

They added: “Many police forces hold this data not only from suspects, but from potential victims and witnesses of crimes.”

Several other applications within Palantir Nectar make use of forensically analysed device data. One has been specifically designed to support a national policing operation targeting Western Balkan organised crime and immigration offences. It appears that the AI has been trained to “recognise images of cocaine and cannabis” found in extracted devices, according to previous reports.

Another application within Nectar provides “AI-supported mobile phone analysis and translation” of extracted device data.

The system also analyses sensitive personal data, including people’s political opinions, religious beliefs and sexual orientations, according to previous reports.

Concerns have been raised that “like any AI system, the outputs depend on the data fed into it” that “reflect historic and existing biases within these institutions and across wider society”, according to Alamara Khwaja Bettum, executive director of civil liberties charity Statewatch.

This will likely “lead to over-policing and criminalisation of marginalised communities, particularly racialised groups, migrants and people from low-income neighbourhoods”.

One of the data sources for Palantir Nectar – a system called Athena – contained more than 1,000 records for individuals in 2025 who had not been charged with any crimes, according to freedom of information disclosures to Computer Weekly. Any of this sensitive personal data could be analysed by Nectar’s AI processing if investigators were to choose to do so.

Privacy International said that this risks “disproportionate and unnecessary use of personal data, inaccuracy, data security, and the rights of freedoms of individuals”, which Bedfordshire Police has itself acknowledged in internal documents.

The campaign group continued that the police force’s decision to use Nectar to “expand its surveillance capabilities by exploiting deeply intrusive data about individuals, without concern for [Palantir’s] human rights record, and without fully explaining how the data will be used or how many people this project will affect, raises serious legal and ethical concerns”.

Bedfordshire Police is leading the Palantir Nectar pilot within the Eastern Regional Special Operations Unit (ERSOU), a joint policing unit tackling serious organised crime and terrorism. Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire constabularies have access to the platform through Bedfordshire Police. These forces, alongside Essex, Kent, Norfolk and Suffolk constabularies, make up the rest of the ERSOU. The pilot is in preparation for a national roll-out of the software.

The pilot is being partially audited by Accenture. This same consultancy firm has recently announced a “global strategic partnership” with Palantir, acquired a company that helps organisations implement Palantir’s software, and is part of the same consortium earning from the multimillion-pound NHS contract.

Representatives for Accenture acknowledged Computer Weekly’s queries but failed to respond.

Bedfordshire Police did not answer questions about whether it considered a conflict of interest in having Accenture audit its pilot, given that the firm could stand to gain from Palantir obtaining further government contracts, but a spokesperson said the force is also evaluating the project internally.

Bedfordshire Police said it is “imperative” that police systems evolve to “provide a service the public expects” given the changing policing landscape. The number of domestic violence disclosures has also trebled as a result of the Palantir Nectar pilot, according to the force. An ethics panel composed of police officials and academics is providing “independent scrutiny” of AI use, while the police and crime commissioner is also establishing an Artificial Intelligence Advisory Ethics Panel.

A Palantir spokesperson said the firm is “proud” the software is fighting crime. “But that is what it is – software. How that software is used to process data is entirely under the control of the customer. Critically, use of the software does not involve acquiring any data that the customer in question doesn’t already have access to – it simply organises that data in a way that enables faster, better decision-making.”

Palantir also confirmed to Computer Weekly that its software has been used by the US military for airstrike targeting in Iran.

“Palantir has developed its technologies by testing them in war-torn countries and using them in the genocide in Palestine,” according to Romain Lanneau, a legal consultant at Statewatch. “Based on that alone, the UK should consider any collaboration with Palantir highly unethical.”

Leicestershire Police is also leading a Palantir Nectar trial within the East Midlands Special Operations Unit (EMSOU), which includes Derbyshire, Lincolnshire, Northamptonshire and Nottinghamshire Police.

London mayor Sadiq Khan recently blocked the Metropolitan Police’s £50m deal with Palantir as the proposal had not “ensured or demonstrated value for money”, although the force has been able to continue using it for the next year.

Police plans to integrate IT systems

Police chiefs had previously expressed concerns about reliance on the multiplicity of commercial and in-house platforms such as Palantir Nectar, Prometheus and BAE Systems’ Intelligence Lead Assessment Service, and existing systems such as the Police National Database, which risk “excessive costs” and “architectural incoherence” given that they would all be using the same data, according to documents obtained by Computer Weekly.

The solution, therefore, was to bring all of the police’s data exploitation and collation tools under one roof.

“The National Data and Analytics Office is working to centralise the way in which forces utilise data and procure data exploitation technology – to reduce duplicated investment and again, protect forces against the risks [mentioned],” the NDAO’s Fisher-Stevens told Computer Weekly.

Following on from London City Hall blocking the Met’s £50m contract with Palantir, commissioner Mark Rowley warned against the constraints of public procurement policy on the police’s ability to deploy emerging technology effectively. Rowley said the force stands to gain from being able to “connect” and “spot patterns at the touch of a button” across the force’s 2,200 datasets held in over 600 systems.

The NDIES appears to answer this concern, giving the police access to a wide range of national intelligence in an organised way. Yet the underlying risks raised by campaign groups on biases within the data and the invasive nature of collection remain. “The question is whether it can possibly be necessary and proportionate,” according to Privacy International.

UK police are developing a national service for sharing local intelligence and police force data across the law enforcement and justice estate.

Announced by the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) earlier this year, the National Data Integration and Exploitation Service (NDIES) will allow local police forces to access and share data, including local force intelligence and digital forensics, from across the country.

Privacy campaigners have raised concerns that the project could facilitate artificial intelligence (AI)-powered analysis of bulk datasets of personal information which, when considered alongside facial recognition and other forms of real-time tracking, shows how “powerful” state surveillance apparatus is.

A “police data factory” within NDIES will incorporate data from over 50 law enforcement agencies, the Home Office, the Ministry of Justice, and “other” partners to provide them with access to a vast network of data for “analytical and reporting purposes”. These government departments will not be able to see operational data or intelligence itself, according to the NPCC.

Computer Weekly can also reveal exclusive details about key data exploitation systems used by several police forces expected to “plug into” NDIES datasets, including:

  • A planned national roll-out of software that will facilitate deep analysis of forensically extracted mobile phone data.
  • Internal Bedfordshire Police memos that admit there is a “medium risk” that a system provided by the US-based data analytics firm Palantir will potentially process personal data for purposes that are neither proportionate nor necessary.
  • Datasets feeding Bedfordshire Police’s Palantir system contain more than 1,000 records on people who haven’t been charged with crimes.

The National Data Integration and Exploitation Service

The National Data and Analytics Office (NDAO) within the NPCC is delivering the NDIES in collaboration with the Home Office. Kate Fisher-Stevens, director of the NDAO, has said the aim is “not to create a single national platform, collect more data or share it unnecessarily” but to “ensure data can be collated when necessary”.

“The creation of a centralised data infrastructure that supports cross-force, cross-system data sharing will be pivotal to that aim – creating a single version of the truth, with time, resource and subsequent cost significantly reduced,” she said.

In a pre-market engagement tender published last year, the capabilities for the NDIES were expected to cost between £75m and £250m over five years.

title: Technology teams to be hit by Visa’s 7% jobs cull
raw_text:
Visa will cut 7% of its workforce and increase the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to “evolve” how it works, according to an internal memo to staff.

In his message to over 34,000 employees, reported by Bloomberg, Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said its technology and product teams will primarily be affected by the 2,600 job cuts.

The CEO wrote: “I have deep conviction that we are doing what is right for Visa, our clients and our partners as we continue to focus on driving efficiency across the company in order to reinvest in our highest potential opportunities.”

He told staff that AI is being used to change how employees work. “To capture the opportunities ahead and best position Visa to lead this transformation, we must continue evolving how we work,” wrote McInerney. “AI is also helping to accelerate this evolution and shape the way work gets done at Visa.”

Quoting a person with knowledge of the company’s decision, Bloomberg reported that AI is not the only driver of the job cuts, with Visa keen to reinvest in “consumer payments, commercial and money-movement solutions and value-added services, which include stablecoin, cross-border and business-to-business offerings”.

According to an independent benchmarking report in February, AI has already become institutionalised at Visa, and the firm is leading the way in the technology’s application in the payments sector.

The report from benchmarking company Evident ranked Visa number one in its AI index for payments, as a result of what it described as its shift from individual AI use cases to “institutional capability”.

Read more about AI in finance

  • AI-related roles could be the only ‘safe jobs’ in the banking sector as financial organisations ‘relentlessly’ press on with AI-led transformation.
  • The payment card services giant leads the way in applying artificial intelligence in its sector, according to research.

Mastercard came in at number two, while PayPal took third spot in the index of 12 payments companies, which documented nearly 100 use cases for AI in the payments sector.

But, according to Evident, payments firms have not detailed their return on investment from AI spend, unlike banks.

The index took into account four factors: talent, innovation, leadership and transparency. According to Evident, Visa demonstrates the clearest evidence that AI is institutionalised across its core transaction network.

“What sets Visa apart is the degree to which the company is demonstrating impact at scale over multiple years from applications of AI across its operations and network,” said Evident co-founder Alexandra Mousavizadeh at the time of the report. “It signals a shift from individual use cases to AI as an institutional capability.”

But unlike banks, Evident said no payments company has disclosed realised or projected return on investment across all AI investments. Also speaking at the time of the report, Evident’s other co-founder, Annabel Ayles, said this is “increasingly conspicuous”.

“While one in five banks now report on group-level AI returns, payments firms have yet to quantify the aggregate impact of their AI investments,” she said. “To keep justifying this expenditure, the market will sooner or later demand clearer evidence of value.”

Banks are gaining huge benefits from AI today, with Lloyds Banking Group’s Financial institutions sentiment survey for 2025 finding that 59% of surveyed firms reported AI-driven productivity gains in the past 12 months, compared with 32% in the 2024 survey.

title: Did an AI agent really break free and attack another company?
raw_text:
Did artificial intelligence (AI) just break out of its sandbox, hack another company and go rogue? That is certainly how some of the reporting around the recent Hugging Face incident has portrayed it. But the reality is more complicated – and perhaps more worrying.

What happened was not an AI spontaneously deciding to escape and launch a cyber attack, it was the result of an experiment designed to test the limits of highly capable AI models, with some of the safeguards that would normally prevent them from conducting high-risk cyber activity apparently deliberately removed.

What happened?

Earlier in July, a story emerged claiming that a rogue AI model had been involved in the hacking of Hugging Face, an AI model-hosting platform. In a blog post published on 16 July, Hugging Face said the attack “was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system”.

In particular, the company claimed that a malicious dataset abused two code execution paths in its dataset processing system to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor was able to escalate to node-level access, collect cloud and cluster credentials, and move laterally into several internal clusters over the course of a weekend.

Hugging Face further claimed the campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework, appearing to be built on an agentic security research harness. This was able to execute thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control (C2) infrastructure staged on public services.

OpenAI subsequently acknowledged that its models had been responsible for the activity. In a blog post published five days later, on 21 July, it said the incident occurred during an internal evaluation of advanced cyber capabilities, where models were given fewer safeguards to assess how effectively they could identify and exploit vulnerabilities.

Once they had access, the models identified ways to reach Hugging Face infrastructure and obtain information that could help them bypass the security evaluation. This included using stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities to find a route to remote code execution (RCE) on Hugging Face’s servers.

What we learned from the incident

The primary questions raised by the incident are whether or not this was the first instance in which we have lost control of an AI agent and seen it go rogue to attack a company, where the guardrails were in this incident, and what the future learnings are for companies from an incident such as this.

OpenAI describes the incident as “unprecedented in terms of the cyber capabilities demonstrated”, according to the Hugging Face blog. It also says it is sharing its preliminary findings to help defenders understand the emerging risks posed by increasingly capable AI models.

Hugging Face claims that the incident matches the “agentic attacker” scenario the industry has been forecasting, and that autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical.

“It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed,” it claims. “Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface and using AI on defence to keep pace.”

If you were not already considering your data and model as an attack surface, this must surely be a catalyst to better protect them. Security consultant Brian Honan, CEO of BH Consulting, says that whenever software accepts content from external users and executes code as part of processing that content, it creates an area of elevated risk.

“The important question isn’t simply whether the code execution path existed, but whether it was sufficiently isolated, monitored and designed on the assumption that malicious content would eventually be submitted,” he explains.

“Security controls such as sandboxing, strong privilege separation, limiting what executed code can access, continuous monitoring, behavioural detection and regular security testing all help reduce the likelihood that a vulnerability can be successfully exploited or that an attacker can move beyond the initial point of compromise.”

In this case, the AI agent was being tested internally on hacking capabilities in a sandboxed environment, but the models were able to gain open internet access by locating a previously undiscovered vulnerability.

Jake Moore, global cyber security advisor at ESET, points to a “worrying lack of human interaction” in this instance, as well as the apparent absence of some basic security methodology from the testing environment.

He points out that the situation was clearly not completely contained, and that it was not fully sandboxed or air-gapped as it should have been.

“It cannot be called a containment or a sandboxed environment because it has no access,” says Moore. “We create sandboxes on purpose to keep malicious software completely hidden from the network. So, if there was any way out, that was OpenAI’s fault.”

Moore adds that every time one AI system discovers something, other models can learn from it laterally, with models continually being updated based on their inputs and outputs. He described this as “a huge beast that is effectively getting out of control”.

This means the way these models work needs to be rethought, explains Moore, with both models and security teams needing to continually learn, adapt and evolve as we become accustomed to using increasingly powerful systems.

“I know technology moves quickly, but yeah, this is outrageously quick,” he adds.

Moore describes AI as a “cheeky, younger brother” that doesn’t ask for permission and is going to test what it can do. “Therefore, I do think that AI will go rogue more often, because it’s got the ability to, and in my eyes, can do anything that it wants to,” he says. “It’s just that we’re going to notice, talk about and write about the illegalities of that, which are still really difficult to safeguard and bake into these algorithms.”

What we know overall is that AI tools need appropriate safeguards in place, and for some reason, those safeguards appear not to have been sufficient in this case. It may be that the security guardrails were deliberately relaxed as part of the testing process. However, Hugging Face’s CEO, Clément Delangue, subsequently posted on social media that he is seeking $100m (£75.2m) in compute from OpenAI to help the Hugging Face community build powerful cyber defences using the best open and closed models.

Delangue argues that, as the first autonomous agent cyber attack is an unprecedented event, “it deserves an unprecedented response”.

Future learnings

From Delangue’s statements, it is clear that more research is needed into what AI can actually do. Despite all the talk about AI’s capabilities, it is becoming clear these systems may be more powerful than even experts could have conceived. The fact that the models were apparently able to escape a sandbox, capture credentials and breach a company without direct human intervention should be taken seriously.

This should lead companies to assume that their agents will evolve and surprise them with their capabilities. They should update governance to define what agents are permitted to do, who is accountable when they don’t follow those boundaries, and how they can be shut off.

They should also invest in detecting anomalous behaviour, because an agent may pursue its assigned goal relentlessly, including by attempting to circumvent the constraints placed upon it. According to Luta Security, the responsibility is to stop it before it actually “hacks the planet”.

Jake Moore says this sort of incident was expected, describing it as “the next phase of security where organisations are facing these incredible threats – not just criminals, but from Frontier AI”.

Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), says there are two important lessons for the future from the incident. The first is to treat current and future generations of models as we would their biological equivalents: in controlled environments with multiple safeguards, comprehensive real-time monitoring and emergency procedures.

The second is the imperative for AI systems to be secure by design and default. The initial breach reinforces the need for upfront threat modelling, and secure-by-design and secure-by-default practices as we build and adopt AI.

As Whitehouse says, while frontier models are impressive, it is a human responsibility to ensure the outcomes we seek are achieved on both sides.

According to a Chatham House report, AI experts have warned for decades that a machine given a task without sufficient guardrails may pursue its goals in unexpected or dangerous ways. The hacking of Hugging Face by OpenAI’s models appears to be an example of precisely this kind of misalignment.

Our main learning here should be that AI is powerful and, without appropriate guardrails, can behave in unexpected ways. Knowledge needs to be built now to ensure that such an incident does not happen again, and that both the company operating the AI agent and any potential victims understand what has happened, how it happened and how to recover.

The question here is not whether AI has suddenly become sentient and turned on its creators: it is whether we are becoming too comfortable giving increasingly capable AI systems the opportunity to discover what they can do when the guardrails come off.

title: The departmental deckchairs have been shuffled – but helping the government's tech challenge how?
raw_text:
It’s been a week since the axe fell on the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT). What have we learned and, critically, are all things tech policy and delivery in a better place now than they were before the new prime minister’s cull?

It’s self-evident that when the department was brought into being it created a clear “route in” for tech businesses small and large and to all those looking for a simple point of access into government. This has now gone.

Last week in the House of Lords, we sought some rationale from the government for this move.

My colleague Tim Clement-Jones raised the issue, asking specifically what the implications would be for the future operation of organisations such as the AI Security Institute, the Government Digital Service (GDS) and UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

The minister's response stressed that “science and AI are having an increasingly large impact on all areas of government policy and economic growth” and should not be seen as isolated from other areas.

This was given as the reasoning for what the minister described as “a bold restructuring, including the elevation of AI to the [newly established] Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet (OPMC).”

The government also published a Written Ministerial Statement setting out the changes, describing the redistribution of DSIT functions as designed to “align with our core economic and social agenda, embedded as vital engines of growth exactly where they can have the most direct impact.”

AI taskforce

There will be a new AI Taskforce within the OPMC, supported by the prime minister's adviser on AI, intended to implement “a strategic, whole-of-government approach [to AI] from the centre.” We now know that it will be Patrick Vallance – who recently departed from government as minister - who will chair this group. That is a very good thing and I hope he can gain traction and cut through in this landscape which has been rendered increasingly complex as a consequence of last week’s changes.

The Cabinet Office will take the lead on AI adoption across the Civil Service and will have responsibility for AI strategy, public sector AI adoption and the AI Security Institute.

Digital, with a capital D, returns to the renamed Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) which gains responsibility for “digital foundations, digital transformation, digital inclusion and skills, GDS, information resilience and online harms”. The government said that this will bring “coherence to the online safety agenda”.

The GDS move is particularly problematic. GDS built whatever authority it has over the last decade by sitting close enough to the centre to mandate standards across departments that would otherwise happily ignore it. The move to DCMS reduces GDS authority - GDS’s view - to that of a single department with the ability to, well, try and influence other departments of its view. If might is right, as is so often the case within Whitehall, the very best of British with that.

Just when you thought you had a grip on the departmental acronyms, another one emerges. The Department for Business and Trade is gone, becoming the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), taking on responsibility for the science and innovation portfolio, as well as emerging sectors.

Keeping up so far? There’s more:

The Cabinet Office, having gained some new functions, will lose the Office for Equality and Opportunity, which moves to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.

The Office for the Impact Economy and responsibility for policy on digital identity will move to DCMS.

The Public Sector Fraud Authority will move to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) with continued central sponsorship from HM Treasury. And the Investment Security Unit will move to DBIST.

Many questions

During our Lords debate, regret was expressed about the resignation of minister Vallance who will be much missed, though, as stated above, he has already re-appeared as the AI taskforce chair.

Many questions were raised about the changes, including responsibility for AI regulation, the "waste of time" and difficulties maintaining momentum on AI safety and sovereignty during the transition, the wrong signal being sent to the science community and the potential erosion of funding for basic science.

The severing of digital infrastructure from AI sovereign investment is also more than unfortunate. Prior to the change we had one department with effective oversight of these so clearly linked areas. This has been exchanged for a yet to be constructed coordination between different departments, with different ministers, with different incentives – is that really better?

It is positive that we are retaining Kanishka Narayan as AI minister and that he will attend Cabinet. But does he have a full picture of what is under his ministerial responsibility and who he reports to and in what order?

With all this change in Whitehall I do have cause to wonder whether a cross-sector, cross-economy AI regulation bill is more likely today than before the current PM’s arrival? Here’s hoping.

To conclude, I can’t improve upon the comments of Laura Gilbert, former director of the AI Incubator at Number 10, on hearing news of the changes:

"So now a new government has again come in, the very week that those affected by the last machinery of government [change] finally transitioned to new laptops, and what did they do? Did they arrive, ask questions, learn about what had not worked before and why, consult with people with government and technical expertise, understand the problems and carefully and thoughtfully design a solution? Or did they do the exact same thing the last two governments did to the exact same people, the thing that evidently they felt had failed to the point of needing fixing, and then pat themselves on the back?"

And, if they think it’s all over - it isn’t yet. As Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Select Committee chair Chi Onwurah said, she expects her committee to “look into the impact of closing DSIT, and how science, innovation and technology can best be coordinated across government in the absence of a dedicated department” in the autumn.

She welcomed the government’s ambition to embed science and tech across the economy but said splitting up DSIT risks “fragmenting” policies and “overloading departments that may lack capacity to give them the attention they need.”

That may well all be true, time et al will tell. One thing we can know for sure at this stage is that, as a consequence of the changes, when we all return in the autumn, the chair will be responsible for the BIST Select Committee in Parliament.

title: Bahrain cannot claim sovereign immunity for spyware attack against UK dissidents, top UK court rules
raw_text:
The Kingdom of Bahrain cannot claim sovereign immunity to legal action brought by two Bahraini dissidents who accuse it of infecting their computers with German-made spyware, the UK’s Supreme Court has ruled.

The dissidents, Saeed Shehabi and Moosa Mohammed, allege that the Kingdom of Bahrain infected their computers with FinFisher spyware while they were living in London in 2011.

The Supreme Court’s decision is expected to open the way for further legal action against countries that target people living in the UK with surveillance software, said Ida Aduwa, solicitor at law firm Leigh Day, which brought the case.

“This ruling sends a clear message to overseas states that use intrusive surveillance technology against peaceful political activists and others that they will face justice in the courts,” she said.

The Kingdom of Bahrain claimed that under the State Immunity Act 1978, sovereign states had immunity in cases where the perpetrators, or some of the acts, causing personal injury were not located in the UK.

But the Supreme Court, with a majority of three to two, found that modern technology enables surveillance to be carried out remotely, and that even if a foreign state conducted a surveillance operation from outside the UK, it would still involve an infringement of UK territorial sovereignty.

Shehabi, 71, a journalist and founder of Bahraini opposition party Al Wefaq, and Mohammed, a pro-democracy activist, allege that their laptops were infected in September 2011 with malicious surveillance software known as FinSpy, made by the Gamma group.

They claim the attacks allowed Bahraini authorities to collect information from their laptops, including messages, emails, calendar records, contact lists, browsing history, photos, databases, documents and videos. 

The software also enabled Bahrain to track the location of their laptops and covertly eavesdrop on conversations by using the laptop’s microphones and cameras.

The activists learned that their computers had been hacked in 2014 when WikiLeaks published documents about Bahrain’s use of FinSpy and a research and advocacy organisation, Bahrain Watch, identified them as victims of hacking.

Bahrain opposition to Shehabi and Mohammed

The Bahraini government has repeatedly denounced Shehabi – who has lived in the UK since 1973 and gained British citizenship in 2002 – over his political activism. In 2009, his home in the UK was set on fire shortly after two associates who had campaigned against the Bahraini government were beaten up outside London Euston railway station.

Mohammed, 45, a photographer, videographer and human rights activist, was repeatedly arrested, detained, tortured and mistreated by the police after taking part in protests in Bahrain. He fled to the UK in 2006 as a refugee, and has since been granted indefinite leave to remain in the UK.

The Bahraini government has publicly condemned him for helping to organise protests in the UK and publishing accounts of human rights abuses in the Kingdom.

In 2021, the Bahraini Ministry of Foreign Affairs included Shehabi and Mohammed on a list of Bahraini nationals who have had their Bahraini citizenship revoked.

Bahrain ‘can no longer hide’

Speaking after the verdict, Shehabi said the judgment means the Bahraini regime can no longer hide behind state immunity.

“This is not just a victory for us, but for everyone targeted by authoritarian states beyond their own borders,” he added. “The court’s message is clear: states that abuse people on British soil will be held accountable.”

Mohammed said the verdict changed the balance of power between Bahrain and dissidents.

“Since I was a teenager, the Bahraini regime has tortured, imprisoned and hunted me,” he said. “Even after I found safety in the UK, they pursued me across borders.”

Martyn Day, senior partner of law firm Leigh Day, which represented Shehabi and Mohammed, said the “notion that foreign governments can allegedly use sophisticated spyware to interfere with computers and mobile phones of people living in this country is an outrage”.

The law firm has previously represented people impacted by spyware from Rwanda, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

In the verdict today, Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Hamblen and Lady Simler found in favour of the two claimants. Lord Leggatt and Lord Burrows gave dissenting verdicts.

title: Nvidia pushes ahead with security alliance for AI openness
raw_text:
Nvidia has called on policymakers and business to support open artificial intelligence (AI) models to enable better cyber security.

It announced the industry-wide Open Secure AI just days after Microsoft’s open letter to US policymakers which described openness as “one of the most important paths to AI safety and security”.

In a blog post announcing the new initiative to drive open AI security, Nvidia said that companies and governments should invest in shared open infrastructure for AI defence – datasets, evaluation frameworks, attack simulators and red-teaming tools – similar to how past generations invested in open source software.

In the post, Nvidia said: “For cyber security, open models and open harnesses are essential because they democratise defensive capabilities, increase transparency for defenders, enable cyber defence while protecting data, and complement frontier closed models with customisable, localised controls. Open source enables massively distributed community-driven and self-controlled defence – with no single point of failure.”

The AI chipmaker has taken the decision to drive forward an industry alliance for open AI security, following the recent Hugging Face disclosure of a cyber attack that was driven from end-to-end by an autonomous AI agent system.

The advances in frontier AI models show that the tech sector is now in an arms race as advanced AI models continue to evolve.

Nvidia said the Hugging Face disclosure shows that cyber defence needs to be open, using frontier agentic systems: “When closed AI tools – unable to distinguish attackers from defenders – blocked essential forensic analysis, Hugging Face ran the open-weight GLM 5.2 model on its own infrastructure to analyse more than 17,000 actions and contain the intrusion.  

“That incident showed a practical truth: when defenders cannot inspect, adapt and run advanced AI on their own infrastructure, their ability to respond is constrained at exactly the moment speed matters most,” Nvidia warned. It said companies and countries need open frontier defensive tools and techniques to enable critical industries to build security systems across an ecosystem comprising multiple technology providers to  avoid single points of failure.

The inaugural members of the alliance are: Adobe, Cadence, Capital One, Cisco, Cloudera, Cloudflare, Cognition, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Dell Technologies, DoorDash, Elastic, HPE, Hugging Face, IBM, LangChain, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, Naver, NetApp, Nous Research, OpenClaw, Palantir, Palo Alto Networks, Red Hat, Reflection AI, Salesforce, SAP, SK Telecom, ServiceNow, Siemens, Snowflake, SpacexAI, Synopsys, Thinking Machines Lab and TrendAI.

OpenUK has called on the UK to deliver a home-grown equivalent to the Linux Foundation to promote open source technologies. Its CEO Amanda Brock, said: “The alliance is an appropriate step reinforcing Friday’s open letter message to US policy makers and governments by Microsoft.

“It’s great to see a collective response to the open source security challenge – we’ve been seeing enterprises respond to these issues individually of late, but it’s primarily a US industry response. It’s another example of the future soft power that exists around AI.

“For the UK (like other middle nations) if we want a place at the future dinner table for AI, we need to carve out our own place now. That means sharing and collaborating, but from assets based on intellectual property and collaboration on the technologies that we evolve in country and in our own foundation.”

raw_text: เออร์ไวน์ รัฐแคลิฟอร์เนีย, July 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Tellus Power Global Holding Limited ("Tellus Power" หรือ "บริษัท") บริษัทเทคโนโลยีขั้นสูงซึ่งพัฒนาระบบถ่ายโอนพลังงานแบบสองทิศทาง เพื่อขับเคลื่อนเศรษฐกิจ AI เชิงกายภาพ ประกาศเปิดตัว Tellus Energy AI ในวันนี้ โดยเป็นโมเดล AI ("เฉพาะทาง") ที่ออกแบบมาโดยเฉพาะสำหรับอุตสาหกรรมพลังงานและการประมวลผล โมเดลนี้ออกแบบมาเพื่อประสานการทำงานระหว่างพลังงานและการประมวลผลในหลายทิศทาง โดยจัดสรรภาระการประมวลผล AI ให้สอดคล้องกับความพร้อมใช้งานและราคาไฟฟ้า ณ เวลาจริง พร้อมเปลี่ยนสินทรัพย์ด้านการชาร์จและการกักเก็บพลังงานแบบกระจายศูนย์ให้เป็นทรัพยากรที่ตอบสนองต่อโครงข่ายไฟฟ้าได้ Tellus Power เชื่อว่าบริษัทเป็นหนึ่งในผู้ให้บริการรายแรก ๆ ที่นำการจัดตารางเวลาพลังงานและการประมวลผลแบบหลายทิศทางออกสู่ตลาดภายในโมเดลระดับมืออาชีพเพียงโมเดลเดียว
